claims.text: Machine-learning-based optimization of additive-manufacturing process parameters will improve the dimensional precision of high-entropy-alloy components.
Machine-learning-based optimization will improve the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Machine-learning-based optimization will reduce fabrication-induced defects in additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Optimization of additive-manufacturing parameters reduces thermal gradients.
Optimization of additive-manufacturing parameters reduces residual stresses.
Reduced thermal gradients and residual stresses improve grain structure.
Reduced thermal gradients and residual stresses reduce porosity.
The intervention will produce a 20% improvement in dimensional precision relative to fabrication with default parameters.
The intervention will produce a 15% improvement in mechanical integrity relative to fabrication with default parameters.
The intervention will reduce fabrication-induced defects by 30% relative to fabrication with default parameters.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy-alloy components fabricated by laser powder bed fusion.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy-alloy components fabricated by electron beam melting.
The predicted benefits hold under operating temperatures from -20°C to 100°C and humidity below 60%.
Mechanical integrity will be evaluated by tensile testing at room temperature.
A controlled, replicated experiment will compare machine-learning-optimized parameters with default parameters.

The hypothesis is declared falsified if dimensional precision improves by less than 10%, mechanical integrity improves by less than 5%, or defect density increases by more than 20% relative to default parameters.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifies a 20% dimensional-precision improvement and a 15% mechanical-integrity improvement, but the experiment would not falsify those quantitative predictions unless improvement falls below 10% or 5%, respectively.
The hypothesis requires reduced defects and predicts a 30% reduction, yet the rule permits no reduction—and even an increase of up to 20%—without falsification.
